topic: Supreme Court: why the instructions were wrong

notes: Also states the instructions did not require a link ('nexus') between the persuasion and any particular official proceeding.

notes: DISAGREEMENT/uncertainty: 15 vs 16 analysts depending on the date and list (Thompson says 'Reports indicate'). Use the staff report (C-057) as the main figure and mention the variation.

claim: The staff report found the credit rating agencies kept Enron at 'investment grade' until four days before it filed for bankruptcy; on November 28, 2001 all three agencies cut Enron below investment grade. Enron filed for bankruptcy on December 2, 2001.
quote: On November 28, all three agencies downgraded Enron to below investment grade

locator.section: Part Two II (Credit Rating Agencies); introduction at PDF p. 9 (printed 5)

notes: Bankruptcy date from Batson App. B Part 1, PDF p. 61 (printed 59), which also says the debt was downgraded to junk on Nov 28. Moody's B2, S&P B-, Fitch CC on that date.

claim: Committee staff concluded the rating agencies failed to detect Enron's problems, or take them seriously enough, because they did not exercise proper diligence: they did not ask probing questions or weigh accounting irregularities and complex financing.
quote: the rating agencies failed to detect Enron's problems—or take sufficiently seriously the problems they were aware of—until it was too late because they did not exercise the proper diligence.

topic: Enron's 401(k) match was in Enron stock
claim: GAO testified that Enron matched 50 percent of employees' pre-tax 401(k) contributions up to 6 percent of base pay, with the match invested only in Enron stock, which employees could not move until age 50. Enron's plans covered over 20,000 employees.
quote: with the matching contributions invested solely in the Enron Corporation Stock Fund.
source_type: GAO report (testimony of Comptroller General David Walker)
notes: Enron plan chairman James Prentice testified the stock match was reinstituted in 1998 and restricted until age 50 (C-068).

claim: GAO cited Labor Department figures that 63 percent of Enron's 401(k) assets were invested in company stock at the end of 2000.
quote: DOL reports that 63 percent of Enron's 401(k) assets were invested in company stock as of the end of 2000.
notes: Figure is GAO relaying DOL. No library document I read gives a different percentage.

claim: GAO said Enron's plan fiduciaries imposed a 'lockdown' on the 401(k) plan, blocking withdrawals and transfers while the stock was falling, in order to change recordkeepers, an acceptable practice; but executives faced no similar limits on company stock held outside the plan.
quote: Enron imposed the lockdown to change recordkeepers, an acceptable practice.

locator.section: ERISA Requires Fiduciaries to be Prudent and Reasonable

notes: GAO notes observers questioned whether employees were adequately notified. GAO gives no lockdown dates.

claim: Senator Edward Kennedy, opening the Feb 7, 2002 HELP hearing, said Enron executives cashed out more than $1 billion of stock while workers lost more than $1 billion from their 401(k) plans.
quote: At Enron, executives cashed out more than $1 billion of stock while Enron workers lost more than $1 billion from their 401(k) retirement plans.
notes: A senator's statement, not a finding. Rep. Ken Bentsen at the same hearing said the plan lost 'about $1 billion' (C-065). Use 'about $1 billion' with attribution.

claim: Rep. Ken Bentsen testified the plan lost about $1 billion and that during the lockdown the stock fell from $30.72 at the close on October 16 to $11.69 on November 19, 2001; he described an 'October 16 lockdown' noticed by a letter dated October 8.
quote: Enron Corporation's 401(k) plan lost about $1 billion in value.
source_type: hearing testimony (Member of Congress as witness)
notes: DISAGREEMENT: Fleetham's notice said the lockdown ran Oct 20-Nov 19 (C-066); Lacey said PGE employees were locked out in late September (C-067). State the dates as disputed.

topic: An employee's notice of the lockdown
claim: Former Enron employee Jan Fleetham testified she received on October 15 a letter dated October 8 saying she could not access her account from October 20 to November 19, 2001.
quote: I would be unable to access my account from October 20th to November 19th.

locator.section: Prepared statement of Jan Fleetham (oral version at PDF p. 67, printed 63)

notes: Her sale ordered Oct 9 was confirmed with an Oct 30 withdrawal date and she received a check dated Nov 9 for about 10 percent of what she expected (same page).

topic: Portland General employees locked out earlier
claim: Portland General Electric employee Steve Lacey testified that most PGE employees were 100 percent in Enron stock, that PGE employees could not get into the plan website as early as late September 2001, and that his own losses exceeded $100,000.
quote: So that effectively, we were locked out in late September.

locator.section: Testimony of Steven E. Lacey (begins PDF p. 62)

notes: He speaks only for his own workplace ('I cannot speak for Houston'). Lawsuit he filed is mentioned but not its outcome.

claim: James Prentice, chairman of the Enron Savings Plan's Administrative Committee, testified that employees could choose among 20 investment options, but the company's matching Enron stock, reinstituted in 1998, could not be moved until age 50.
quote: Employees were not permitted to shift the match from Enron to other investment options until they reached the age of 50.
notes: Prentice said he could not address Enron's accounting issues.

claim: Labor Secretary Elaine Chao testified that on November 16, 2001, over two weeks before the bankruptcy, the Labor Department opened an investigation of Enron's pension plans, including the blackout period.
quote: On November 16, 2001, over two weeks before Enron declared bankruptcy, the Department launched an investigation into the activities of Enron's pension plans.

locator.section: Prepared statement of Elaine L. Chao

source_type: prepared statement submitted for the hearing record
notes: Outcome of the DOL investigation is not in the library (gap).

claim: President Bush signed the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (Public Law 107-204) on July 30, 2002; CRS noted some described it as the most important securities legislation since the 1933 and 1934 securities acts.
quote: On July 30, 2002, President Bush signed into law the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, P.L. 107-204.
notes: The 'most important' line is CRS reporting what 'some' said; attribute it. Law text header also shows July 30, 2002.

claim: At the July 30, 2002 signing, President Bush called the law the most far-reaching reform of American business practices since Franklin Roosevelt and said, of accountants, 'The auditors will be audited.'
quote: The auditors will be audited.

locator.section: Remarks on Signing the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (Weekly Comp. Pres. Doc., vol. 38)

notes: Brief allows one short quote. Same page: CEOs and CFOs 'must personally vouch' for disclosures.

claim: Section 101 created the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board to oversee audits of public companies; it is a nonprofit corporation, not a government agency, whose duties include registering audit firms, setting auditing standards and inspecting firms.
quote: There is established the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, to oversee the audit of public companies that are subject to the securities laws

topic: SOX Sec. 101(e): five members, only two CPAs
claim: The PCAOB has five full-time members; two, and only two, must be or have been certified public accountants.
quote: Two members, and only 2 members, of the Board shall be or have been certified public accountants
notes: If a CPA is chair, he or she must not have practiced as a CPA for at least 5 years before appointment.

claim: Section 201 makes it unlawful for a registered audit firm to provide certain non-audit services to a company it audits, including bookkeeping, financial systems design, appraisal, actuarial, internal audit outsourcing, management or HR functions, investment banking, and legal services unrelated to the audit; other non-audit services, including tax, need advance approval by the company's audit committee.
quote: it shall be unlawful for a registered public accounting firm ... to provide to that issuer, contemporaneously with the audit, any non-audit service
notes: Quote contains an ellipsis for omitted words; verbatim otherwise. Connects to the Andersen fee cards (C-019 to C-022).

claim: Section 203 bars an audit firm from auditing a company if its lead audit partner, or the reviewing partner, has done the audit in each of the five previous fiscal years.
quote: has performed audit services for that issuer in each of the 5 previous fiscal years of that issuer.
notes: Compare Andersen's own seven-year rotation (C-036).

claim: Section 302 requires the SEC to make a company's principal executive and financial officers certify each annual and quarterly report: that they reviewed it, that it contains no material untrue statements or omissions, that the financial statements fairly present the company's condition, and that they are responsible for internal controls.
quote: the signing officer has reviewed the report

topic: SOX Sec. 906: criminal penalties for false certification
claim: CRS summarized that Section 906 separately requires CEOs and CFOs to certify periodic reports, with up to $1 million and 10 years for a knowing false certification and up to $5 million and 20 years for a willful one.
quote: would face a fine of up to $5 million, imprisonment of not more than 20 years, or both.
notes: Sec. 906 was not in my brief's list; included because it pairs with Sec. 302 for Chapter 7/Phase 2. Drop if not needed.

claim: Section 404 requires each annual report to include management's statement of responsibility for internal control over financial reporting and an assessment of its effectiveness, and requires the company's auditor to attest to and report on that assessment.
quote: each registered public accounting firm that prepares or issues the audit report for the issuer shall attest to, and report on, the assessment made by the management of the issuer.

claim: Section 802 made it a crime, punishable by up to 20 years, to knowingly destroy or alter records to obstruct a federal investigation or bankruptcy case, including 'in contemplation' of one; it also requires auditors to keep audit workpapers for five years, with up to 10 years' prison for knowing and willful violations.
quote: shall be fined under this title, imprisoned not more than 20 years, or both.
notes: Directly responds to the Andersen shredding. Note the 'in relation to or contemplation of' wording vs. the Supreme Court's nexus concern under Sec. 1512 (C-044). Do not claim Congress intended this link unless a legislative-history source says so.

claim: Section 806 bars public companies from firing, demoting, threatening or harassing employees for lawfully giving information about suspected securities fraud to federal agencies, Congress, or a supervisor, and gives them a civil action.
quote: may discharge, demote, suspend, threaten, harass, or in any other manner discriminate against an employee
notes: Links to the whistleblower chapter (Watkins).

claim: On April 25, 2003, the SEC announced it had determined that the PCAOB was appropriately organized and able to carry out the Act, under Section 101(d); SEC Chairman William Donaldson named founding members Charles Niemeier (acting chairman), Dan Goelzer, Kayla Gillan and Bill Gradison.
quote: the PCAOB has been determined to be appropriately organized and has the capacity to carry out the requirements of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.
notes: Only four members are named although the Act provides for five; the release does not explain the fifth seat. Do not fill it from memory.
